summary.text: Exact divisibility is established prime-by-prime: counting pairs divisible by each \(q^i\) gives the numerator valuation \(\sum_i\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor^2\), while Legendre’s formula and a floor-sum bound place the denominator valuation below it. For \(0\le k<p\), there is no multiple of \(p\) in \((np,np+k]\), so all new gcd factors have zero \(p\)-valuation; factorial valuations are likewise unchanged because they depend on the largest multiple of \(p\) below their arguments and \(\lfloor(np+k)/(rp)\rfloor=\lfloor np/(rp)\rfloor\), while new denominator indices contribute only \(1!\), so subtracting denominator from numerator valuations proves the result.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(m)=\prod_{1\le j\le m}\prod_{1\le \ell\le m}\gcd(j,\ell),
\qquad
D(m)=\prod_{1\le r\le m}\left(\left\lfloor\frac mr\right\rfloor !\right)^r.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)},
\]
where the quotient is ordinary integer division. We will first prove that this division is exact, and then compare the prime exponents in the two factors at the arguments \(np\) and \(np+k\).

Throughout, for a prime \(q\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in \(x\).

## 1. The quotient defining \(a(m)\) is an integer

We establish this because, once exactness is known, we may use
\[
v_q(a(m))=v_q(N(m))-v_q(D(m)).
\]

Fix a prime \(q\). For positive integers \(j,\ell\), the exponent of \(q\) in their gcd is
\[
v_q(\gcd(j,\ell))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j\ \text{and}\ q^i\mid\ell}.
\]
Indeed, if \(e=v_q(\gcd(j,\ell))\), then precisely the powers \(q,q^2,\ldots,q^e\) divide both \(j\) and \(\ell\). All sums over \(i\) here are finite, since terms vanish once \(q^i>m\).

Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(N(m))
&=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{\ell=1}^m v_q(\gcd(j,\ell))\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\#\{1\le j\le m:q^i\mid j\}
                    \#\{1\le \ell\le m:q^i\mid \ell\}\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
The last equality uses the elementary fact that the number of multiples of a positive integer \(Q\) in \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is \(\lfloor m/Q\rfloor\).

For the denominator, Legendre's formula gives
\[
v_q(t!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D(m))
&=\sum_{r=1}^m r\,v_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac mr\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{r=1}^m r\sum_{i\ge1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/r\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{r=1}^m
 r\left\lfloor\frac{m}{r q^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
Here we used the standard identity
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/r\rfloor}{Q}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{rQ}\right\rfloor
\]
for positive integers \(r,Q\).

We now prove the floor-sum estimate
\[
\sum_{r=1}^m r\left\lfloor\frac{m}{rQ}\right\rfloor
\le \left\lfloor\frac mQ\right\rfloor^2
\tag{3}
\]
for every positive integer \(Q\). Put \(s=\lfloor m/Q\rfloor\). If \(r>s\), then \(rQ>m\), so \(\lfloor m/(rQ)\rfloor=0\). Thus only \(1\le r\le s\) contribute. For each such \(r\), set \(u=\lfloor m/(rQ)\rfloor\). Since \(urQ\le m\), we have
\[
(ru)Q\le m,
\]
and hence \(ru\le\lfloor m/Q\rfloor=s\). There are \(s\) possible contributing values of \(r\), and every summand is at most \(s\). Therefore their sum is at most \(s^2\), proving (3).

Apply (3) with \(Q=q^i\) in (2). We obtain
\[
v_q(D(m))
\le\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2
=v_q(N(m))
\]
by (1). This is true for every prime \(q\). Since both products are positive (and for \(m=0\) both are empty products equal to \(1\)), the prime factorization criterion for divisibility yields
\[
D(m)\mid N(m).
\tag{4}
\]
Thus \(a(m)=N(m)/D(m)\) is an integer for every \(m\), and for every prime \(q\),
\[
v_q(a(m))=v_q(N(m))-v_q(D(m)).
\tag{5}
\]

## 2. No new multiple of \(p\) occurs inside the block

Now let \(n\ge1\), let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy \(0\le k<p\). Set
\[
M_0=np,\qquad M_1=np+k.
\]
There is no multiple of \(p\) strictly between \(M_0\) and \(M_1\). More explicitly, if
\[
np<x\le np+k,
\]
then \(p\nmid x\). For if \(p\mid x\), then \(p\mid x-np\). But
\[
0<x-np\le k<p,
\]
whereas a positive integer divisible by \(p\) must be at least \(p\), a contradiction.

We will also need the following consequence. If \(E>0\) and \(p\mid E\), then
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{E}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{E}\right\rfloor.
\tag{6}
\]
To see this, put \(u=\lfloor np/E\rfloor\). If the quotient increased after adding \(k\), then the next multiple \((u+1)E\) would satisfy
\[
np<(u+1)E\le np+k.
\]
But \((u+1)E\) is divisible by \(p\), contradicting the preceding paragraph. Hence the quotient cannot increase, and (6) follows.

## 3. Stability of the numerator

We claim
\[
v_p(N(np+k))=v_p(N(np)).
\tag{7}
\]
The product defining \(N(np+k)\) contains all factors already occurring in \(N(np)\), together with factors \(\gcd(j,\ell)\) for which at least one of \(j,\ell\) belongs to the new interval
\[
np< x\le np+k.
\]
Every such new index \(x\) is not divisible by \(p\). If, for example, \(p\nmid j\), then \(p\nmid\gcd(j,\ell)\), since every divisor of the gcd divides \(j\). The same holds if the new index is \(\ell\). Therefore every newly introduced gcd has \(p\)-adic order zero. The sum of the \(p\)-adic orders of all gcd factors is consequently unchanged, proving (7).

Equivalently, one can see (7) immediately from (1): for every \(i\ge1\), the denominator \(p^i\) is divisible by \(p\), so (6) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
and hence every term in the power-level formula for \(v_p(N(M))\) is unchanged.

## 4. Stability of the denominator

We next prove
\[
v_p(D(np+k))=v_p(D(np)).
\tag{8}
\]
We separate the old indices \(1\le r\le np\) from the newly appearing indices \(np<r\le np+k\).

First consider an old index \(r\le np\). Let
\[
t_0=\left\lfloor\frac{np}{r}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
t_1=\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{r}\right\rfloor.
\]
We claim that \(v_p(t_0!)=v_p(t_1!)\). By division in stages,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{t_0}{p}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{rp}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac{t_1}{p}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{rp}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because \(rp>0\) and \(p\mid rp\), equation (6) shows that these two quantities are equal. Call their common value \(s\).

Legendre's formula now shows that the two factorial valuations agree. Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(t_0!)
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =s+\sum_{i\ge2}\left\lfloor\frac{t_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor,\\
v_p(t_1!)
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t_1}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =s+\sum_{i\ge2}\left\lfloor\frac{t_1}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(i\ge2\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{t_j}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor t_j/p\rfloor}{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{s}{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor
\quad(j=0,1),
\]
so all terms coincide. Thus
\[
v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{r}\right\rfloor!\right)
=
v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np}{r}\right\rfloor!\right)
\qquad(1\le r\le np).
\tag{9}
\]
Raising these factorials to the \(r\)-th power multiplies both valuations by the same number \(r\), so the denominator contributions of all old indices are unchanged.

It remains to consider a new index \(r\) satisfying
\[
np<r\le np+k.
\]
We have \(r\le np+k\), so \(\lfloor(np+k)/r\rfloor\ge1\). On the other hand, because \(n\ge1\) and \(p>0\), we have \(p\le np\), and because \(k<p\),
\[
np+k<np+p\le2np<2r.
\]
Therefore \(\lfloor(np+k)/r\rfloor<2\). It follows that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{r}\right\rfloor=1.
\]
The new factor in the denominator is consequently
\[
(1!)^r=1,
\]
which has \(p\)-adic order zero. Combining this fact with (9) proves (8).

## 5. Conclusion

By exact divisibility (4) and the quotient valuation formula (5),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(a(np+k))
&=v_p(N(np+k))-v_p(D(np+k))\\
&=v_p(N(np))-v_p(D(np))\\
&=v_p(a(np)),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the middle equality uses (7) and (8).

Since \(k\) was arbitrary with \(0\le k<p\), this proves
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
=
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))
=
\cdots
=
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1))

\]
for every positive integer \(n\) and every prime \(p\), as claimed.
